analysis.one_liner: Bars OSHA from citing employers on shared work sites for hazards they didn't create or control.
analysis.headline: The bill never left a House subcommittee and died without a vote when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under OSHA rules, an employer on a shared job site — like a general contractor running a construction project — can be cited for a safety violation even if another employer created the hazard. This bill would prohibit that, as long as the employer didn't create the condition, had no employees exposed to it, or hadn't taken on responsibility for compliance by other employers. It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, sent to a subcommittee, and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers on multi-employer work sites, most notably general contractors and site managers on construction projects. They could not be cited by OSHA for unsafe conditions created by subcontractors or other employers, as long as they met any one of three conditions — for example, simply not having created the hazard themselves.
analysis.who_benefits_short: General contractors on shared job sites

how_it_helps.text: The bill would amend the OSH Act so an employer on a multi-employer work site cannot be cited for a violation if it did not create the hazardous condition, had no employees exposed to it, or did not assume responsibility for other employers' compliance [S2].

Because the three conditions are alternatives — an employer qualifies for protection by meeting any one of them — a site-controlling contractor that didn't personally create a hazard and hadn't formally taken on compliance responsibility could escape citation even though OSHA's existing policy treats controlling employers as responsible for site-wide safety.

analysis.who_pays: Workers on shared job sites, especially in construction. If no employer can be cited for a hazard created by someone else and not formally assumed by anyone, responsibility for dangerous conditions can fall through the cracks, weakening the main enforcement lever that keeps multi-employer sites safe.

drawbacks.text: The bill responds to a real complaint: under OSHA's multi-employer policy, an employer can be cited and penalized for a hazard it did not create and had no employees exposed to, which employers argue is unfair punishment without fault [S2].

An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the change would weaken the strongest safety incentive on shared sites. General contractors control access, scheduling, and site conditions; letting them escape citation for subcontractor hazards removes pressure to police overall site safety, and workers would bear that risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill fixes a genuine fairness gripe — punishing employers for hazards they didn't create — but its drafting goes far beyond that fix. Because an employer is protected by meeting any single condition, the site controller with the most power over overall safety could often avoid citation entirely, and the burden of that gap falls on the workers exposed to the hazard. As written, the protection for employers outweighs the fairness correction.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to committee, then to a subcommittee, and sat there until the 106th Congress ended in January 2001, so it died without any vote or hearing in the record.

narrative.text: Rep. Ralph Hall of Texas, joined by Rep. Tauzin, introduced the bill on July 27, 2000, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S1][S3][S5].
On September 20, 2000, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where it stayed with no further action in the record [S5].
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and the bill was never reported out of committee or brought to a floor vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers on shared job sites, because the existing OSHA multi-employer citation policy was left intact; the bill died before employers could gain protection from site-wide liability.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Construction workers; the safety rule survived

for.name: Rep. W.J. Tauzin
for.what_they_did: Joined Hall in introducing the bill, per the bill text

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it; it was never reported out

against.name: Subcommittee on Workforce Protections
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on September 20, 2000, and no hearings or markups appear in the record before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: A Democratic sponsor introduced it with Republican cosponsors [S3][S4], but the bill never reached a vote, so no party split was ever tested.

industries.industry: General contractors and site-controlling employers on multi-employer work sites
industries.note: The bill would have shielded them from OSHA citations for hazards created by other employers on the site. Their gain is workers' loss: less legal pressure on whoever controls the site to fix or prevent dangerous conditions.

industries.industry: Subcontractors and other employers sharing work sites
industries.note: Subcontractors that create hazards would still be citable, so the bill would not fully shield them. Employers across a site would face less exposure to citations for hazards they didn't create, but also less pressure from controlling employers to keep the site safe.
